proposals.relationship: Gellner uses Ibn Khaldun’s dynastic-cycle model to interpret the coexistence of tribal and urban power in Morocco.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1961review explicitly applies the analysis rather than merely praising a precursor. Alatas2006p789also identifies a later fusion with Hume in Gellner’s Muslim reform model; Hume retains separate credit, not an Ibn-only explanation. No precise Muqaddimah edition for Gellner’s1961reading is established; originalArabic and complete Muslim Society unread.

proposals.evidence_note: Named mediation: Malešević2021p394attributes the regional limit and quotes Muslim Society1981p88. His own following argument about modern conditions is kept separate. proposals.relationship: Gellner contrasts Khaldunian dynastic cycles with a Marxian account of colonial capitalism while arguing that both patterns coexist in Morocco.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1961comparison, not a claim that Marx inherited the model. Gellner’s two historical frameworks coexist rather than one simply replacing the other. His interpretation is attributed; neither all Marx nor the full Muqaddimah was read.
primary_locators: Printed386first two paragraphs: This circular destiny through the two existed side by side within one country.

proposals.relationship: Gellner and Dale compare Ibn Khaldun with Durkheim on social cohesion and the explanatory study of society, retaining differences in context and normative aims.
proposals.evidence_note: Gellner’s1975opening extract and Dale’s2006pp442–444supply distinct comparisons. Dale emphasizes shared logical methods and divergent historical conditions. This is their comparison; no direct transmission or medieval membership in modern sociology inferred. Full Durkheim works unread.
